counterfactual_missing_items: No umbilical discharge or cutaneous opening is described to support patent urachus or urachal sinus.
No calcifications, hematuria, or dominant solid enhancing nodule are described to prove malignant transformation.
The 'possible invasion' is uncertain and can be explained by the bladder-dome communication/inflammation of an infected diverticulum.
decisive_items: urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites
a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus
differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant
response.rationale: R1 best reconciles the urachal anatomy (mass arising from the bladder dome and extending toward the umbilicus) with the nitrite-positive lower UTI; a urachal diverticulum is the urachal remnant that communicates with the bladder, causing urinary stasis and persistent cystitis without umbilical discharge. R5 accounts for the multiloculated mass but not the bladder communication/nitrites; R6 overinterprets 'possible invasion' as definite malignancy and lacks classic malignant features; R2 requires umbilical findings; R4 is contradicted by worsening despite antibiotics; C1 is a redundant append-only version of R6.

rejected.why: Initial UTI diagnosis is contradicted by worsening symptoms despite antibiotics and by the CT-detected urachal mass; cannot be the final diagnosis.
Urachal sinus would typically produce an umbilical opening/discharge, which is absent, and it lacks the bladder communication needed to explain the nitrite-positive UTI.
Urachal cyst explains the multiloculated midline mass but not the bladder communication/positive nitrites; it is less complete given the documented urinary infection.
Possible invasion and inflammatory stranding are concerning but nonspecific; without calcifications, definite solid component, or hematuria, an infected urachal diverticulum is more likely.
Append-only completion duplicating R6's 'possible invasion' raw span; it adds no independent evidence and asserts bladder invasion as fact when the raw wording is only 'possible'.
